# Gradle Version Catalog and Dependencies

AniTrend v2 uses Gradle’s **Version Catalog (libs.versions.toml)** to manage dependency versions centrally. The file `gradle/libs.versions.toml` contains all version numbers and coordinates for dependencies and plugins[40][41]. For example, the version of **Kotlin**, **Android Gradle plugin**, and libraries like Koin, Retrofit, etc., are defined there. The project uses the type-safe accessors `libs.` – e.g., `libs.androidx.room.runtime` – to declare dependencies in build scripts instead of hardcoding versions[42].

When adding or upgrading a library, update `libs.versions.toml`: - Add a version under `[versions]` if new. - Add a coordinate under `[libraries]` (or `[plugins]` for Gradle plugins) referencing that version. Then you can use `libs.your.library.id` in the build files. This ensures consistency and easy version management across modules.

## buildSrc: Custom Build Logic

The project has a `buildSrc` **module** (located at `/buildSrc/src/main/java/co/anitrend/buildSrc`) which contains Kotlin code that customizes the build process. This is a common pattern to avoid repetitive Gradle configuration by writing it in Kotlin once and reusing it.

Key components in `buildSrc`: - **Modules.kt** – Defines enumerations of module names and paths for each category (App, Domain, Data, etc.)[3][4]. This provides a single source of truth for module Gradle paths. For example, `Modules.Feature.Media.path` is `":feature:media"`, and `Modules.Data.Tmdb.path` is `":data:tmdb"`. The build scripts and dependency logic use these to include modules. - **Libraries.kt** – Maps some module groups to `Modules` paths (it appears to group AniTrend common libraries like `AniTrend.CommonUi.character = Modules.Common.Character.path`). This might be used to easily include sets of modules. - **Gradle Plugins (in** `buildSrc/plugins`**):** The project defines a custom **CorePlugin** (`co.anitrend.buildSrc.plugins.CorePlugin`) which is applied to every module’s Gradle script. This plugin orchestrates applying the standard Android/Kotlin plugins and our custom configurations. - When applied, `CorePlugin` calls several extension functions: `configurePlugins`, `configureAndroid`, `configureOptions`, `configureDependencies`, etc.[43]. These are defined under `buildSrc/plugins/components/Project*.kt`. - **ProjectPlugins.kt** – Handles applying the base Gradle plugins to each module. For example, it applies `com.android.application` or `com.android.library` depending on if the module is an app module, and always applies the Kotlin Android plugin[44][45]. It also applies the Kotlin Kapt (annotation processor) plugin if the module needs it (e.g., for Room or other annotation processors)[46], and the Kotlin Parcelize plugin for Android extensions if needed. It conditionally applies the Jetpack Compose plugin if the module supports compose (determined by naming conventions)[12]. Additionally, it applies Spotless (code formatter) plugin to all modules. - **ProjectOptions.kt** – Configures Android compile and build options. This sets common **compileSdk, targetSdk, Java compatibility, etc.** (likely in `configureAndroid`, not shown in snippet) and other options. Notably, it injects BuildConfig fields for versioning and secrets: - It reads `versionName` and `versionCode` from project properties (likely from `gradle.properties`) and adds them to all core modules’ BuildConfig[47][48]. - It loads any `.config/secrets.properties` and `.config/configuration.properties` files and adds each property as a `String` field in BuildConfig for data modules[49][50]. This means API keys or secret URLs can be placed in those files (which are not in VCS), and they become accessible via `BuildConfig` constants. For example, a property `ANILIST_API_KEY=abcd` would be injected. - It also sets up the Room compiler options (to export schema, use incremental annotation processing, etc.) for data modules[51][52]. - If a keystore config file exists (`.config/keystore.properties`), it creates a signing config for the release build automatically[53][54]. This allows CI or local builds to sign the APK if provided. - **Product Flavors**: The build uses product flavors (e.g., a "google" flavor). In ProjectPlugins, `configureAdditionalPlugins` shows that if the build variant’s flavor is "google", and a `google-services.json` is present, the Google Services and Crashlytics plugins are applied[55]. This implies there might be at least two flavors (like "google" and "oss" for a variant without Google services, common for F-Droid distribution). The Google flavor enables Firebase analytics and crashlytics. So, when building or adding new features, be mindful of flavor-specific behavior (e.g., some code might be gated behind flavor checks). - **ProjectDependencies.kt** – This is where the magic happens for managing dependencies across modules. Instead of each module declaring its own libraries, this script automatically adds the appropriate dependencies based on module type: - It has functions like `applyFeatureModuleGroupDependencies()`, `applyDataModuleDependencies()`, etc., which add common libraries to those modules. For example, **Feature modules** automatically get all the support-arch UI, domain, data, etc. libraries, AndroidX core libraries, and a dependency on the base app and data modules[56][57]. They also all depend on `:app:core`, `:app:navigation`, `:android:core`, `:domain`, and `:data` modules to have core functionality available. - **App module** (`:app`) gets every other module added (it implements all domain and most data modules) so it bundles the whole app together[58][59]. It also adds core Android dependencies (Material Components, etc.) and things like **LeakCanary** for debug builds[60]. - **Data modules** get Room, Retrofit, OkHttp, paging, etc. automatically[61]. Also the conversion libraries (Kotlin Serialization JSON converter, etc.) and debugging tools like Chucker for networking (added as debug and release dependencies appropriately)[62][63]. KAPT for Room is applied here as well[64]. - **Common, Android, Task modules** each have their own set of common deps (often similar to feature) to ensure they have access to necessary libraries (like core KTX, WorkManager for tasks, etc.)[65][66]. - Compose libraries are added to any module that `hasComposeSupport()` (determined by module name pattern) via `applyComposeDependencies()`[14][67]. This includes all androidx.compose.* libraries, Material3 Compose, navigation-compose, accompanist libraries, etc. So if you create a new feature module (which matches pattern and likely uses Compose), you do **not** need to manually add Compose dependencies – the script will handle it. - The dependency strategy ensures consistency: e.g., all modules get the same version of Kotlin stdlib, and if not a pure domain module, they get Timber for logging by default[68]. It also adds testing libraries (JUnit, MockK) to all modules’ test configurations[69][70]. Koin is added to modules except a few core ones via `applyKoinDependencies()`[70], meaning most modules can use Koin directly.

In summary, **you typically do not add library dependencies in individual module build files** (you may not even find a conventional `dependencies { ... }` block in them). Instead, the `configureDependencies()` function in CorePlugin calls all these apply* functions to add the necessary libraries automatically[71][72]. This results in less duplication and guarantees every module has what it needs. For example, any new `:feature:` module will automatically include Compose, support-arch, core Android libs, etc., by virtue of its name.

- **ProjectSpotless.kt** – Configures the Spotless plugin for code style (Kotlin formatting, perhaps Ktlint). Likely defines the code style rules (indentation, license header, etc.) and is applied to all modules via `configureSpotless()` in CorePlugin[43]. Contributors should run `./gradlew spotlessApply` before committing to auto-format according to these rules. This keeps the code style uniform.
- **PropertiesReader/ProjectProperties** – These likely help read gradle.properties or the custom .properties files from the `.config` directory and provide them via `project.props[...]` as seen in ProjectOptions. It’s a small utility to centralize reading of project properties.
- **ConfigurationResolver.kt** – This is attached to all project configurations to resolve dependency conflicts[73]. For instance, it forces all `kotlin-stdlib` artifacts to use the version defined in our catalog, and similarly aligns versions for serialization, datetime, material components, etc., to avoid runtime conflicts[74][75]. This means if a transitive dependency brings a different version, Gradle will unify it to our chosen version, preventing issues.

## Module Build Files

Each module (e.g., in `app/core/build.gradle.kts`, `feature/../build.gradle.kts`, etc.) is relatively simple because most logic is centralized. Typically, a module’s build script will: - Apply the **CorePlugin** (so that all those config steps run). This might be done with a plugin ID or by `apply<CorePlugin>()` directly. Check the top of module build files: you’ll likely see something like `plugins { id 'com.android.library'; id 'kotlin-android'; /* etc */ }` or an `apply plugin:` usage which triggers CorePlugin. The CorePlugin internally calls our configure functions. - Possibly declare its **module-specific** dependencies or configurations. Most dependencies are auto-added, but if a module has something truly unique (e.g., a feature needs a specific third-party lib that no other module uses), you’d explicitly add it in that module’s dependencies block. For example, a feature that uses a special UI library might add it there. - Sometimes include a `android { ... }` block for things like module-specific build config fields or manifest placeholders. However, much of that (compileSdk, defaultConfig, etc.) might already be set by `configureAndroid()` in CorePlugin. For instance, all modules likely share the same `compileSdkVersion` and Kotlin options configured globally.

Because the **Gradle setup is convention-based**, when adding a new module: - Add the module path in `settings.gradle.kts` with `include(":your:new:module")`. Ensure the folder structure matches (the project has a flat directory structure for modules, organized in subfolders by type). - Define the module’s source in a similar way to others (most are standard Android Library modules except the main app). - Implement the module’s build.gradle.kts similar to an existing one (likely just apply plugins; no need to repeat dependency listings or common configs). - Add the module to `Modules.kt` enumeration under the appropriate category (this is important so that CorePlugin knows it’s a feature, data, etc., and applies the right dependencies). - After this, the buildSrc scripts will automatically do the rest (plugins, dependencies, etc.).

## Build Flavors and Variants

As mentioned, the project has product flavors. Likely **two flavors**: - `google` – includes Google Play Services (Firebase, Crashlytics). Requires `google-services.json` and is used for the Play Store release. - `oss` or a similar flavor – an open-source variant without proprietary services, suitable for F-Droid or development (no analytics, crashlytics). The build logic avoids applying those plugins if not in `google` flavor[55].

Check the `android { productFlavors { ... } }` in the app module for actual names. When writing build configurations or code, be mindful: - Use flavor-specific `AndroidManifest.xml` or resource directories if needed (e.g., a different app name or icon for different flavors). - The code might check `BuildConfig.FLAVOR` or use `BuildConfig.GOOGLE` boolean (sometimes teams add a constant) to turn off features. E.g., analytics logging might be no-op on the OSS flavor. - If adding a new library that’s only used in one flavor, you’d guard its inclusion in buildSrc or module build.gradle using flavor conditions.

## CI and Scripts

The project likely uses GitHub Actions (observing `android-unit-test.yaml` badge in the README[76]). CI will run `./gradlew build` and possibly `./gradlew spotlessCheck`. Ensure your changes do not break the build for all flavors and that code style is correct. There might be a TravisCI config (the README mentions TravisCI, but GitHub Actions badge suggests migration to Actions).

## ProGuard / R8

There is a `proguard-common.pro` in the root[77]. The app may shrink and obfuscate for release. If you add a library that requires keeping certain classes (reflection or serialization), update this proguard file accordingly.

## Summary of Where to Find Things

- **Project-wide settings**: `build.gradle.kts` (root) – global dependency classpath, repositories, conflict resolution (calls `handleConflicts`)[78].
- **Gradle properties**: `gradle.properties` – Java heap settings, org.gradle.jvmargs, and maybe versionCode/versionName definitions.
- **BuildSrc scripts**: in `buildSrc/src/main/java/co/anitrend/buildSrc/` – all custom build logic (if something unusual is happening in the build, look here).
- **Dependency versions**: `gradle/libs.versions.toml` – update library versions here.
- **App Module config**: `app/main/AndroidManifest.xml` for base manifest, `app/core/src/.../Initializer` classes for startup logic (like Koin init).
- **Signing and keys**: not in VCS – `.config/` directory for keystore and API keys. If you are setting up the project, create a `secrets.properties` with dummy API endpoints/keys or ask the project owner for needed keys (the app may require AniList API credentials or not, depending on if they use user-specific tokens – AniList’s API might just use OAuth for user authentication, which could be handled in-app).
- **Gradle tasks**: Standard assemble, install, etc. Custom tasks might not be many since they encapsulated logic in plugins rather than making new tasks. One might be `spotlessApply` (format code). Also, since the project has a lot of modules, using the Gradle **task graph** effectively (like `:app:installGoogleDebug`) will build only what’s needed.

By understanding the build system, you ensure that when you add new code or modules, you integrate seamlessly: - You won’t be surprised by missing dependencies (because buildSrc likely added them). - If something isn’t included, check if your module name fits the expected pattern or if you need to extend buildSrc logic. - Use the existing gradle tasks for consistency (linting, testing, etc., probably configured via Android Gradle Plugin conventions).

Overall, the build setup is quite automated and **convention-driven**. It may take a bit to get used to, but it significantly reduces boilerplate in each module. If in doubt, open `buildSrc/plugins/ProjectDependencies.kt` and see if the library you need is already being added somewhere. This can save you from adding duplicates or the wrong dependency. And remember, the Gradle Kotlin DSL and buildSrc mean that a lot of IntelliSense is available in IDE – you can navigate to functions like `configureDependencies` or constants in Modules.kt easily to understand the configuration.
